methods.label: Construct a route and prove it is shortest
methods.explanation:
Let \(A=(0,0)\), \(B=(12,16)\), and \(O=(6,8)\). The forbidden interior belongs to a circle of radius \(5\). Its center is the midpoint of \(AB\), and
\[
AO=BO=\sqrt{6^2+8^2}=10.
\]
The direct segment passes through the circle, so we need a route around it.

Choose tangent points \(T\) from \(A\) and \(U\) from \(B\) on the same side of line \(AB\). Tangent radii are perpendicular to their tangents, giving
\[
AT=BU=\sqrt{10^2-5^2}=5\sqrt3.
\]
The angle \(\angle AOT\) is \(60^\circ\). To see this without trigonometry, reflect \(O\) across \(T\) to a point \(O'\). Then \(OO'=10\), and the two right triangles on either side of \(AT\) give \(AO'=AO=10\). Thus \(AOO'\) is equilateral. Likewise, \(\angle BOU=60^\circ\).

Since \(OA\) and \(OB\) are opposite rays, the joining arc from \(T\) to \(U\) on the chosen side has central angle
\[
180^\circ-60^\circ-60^\circ=60^\circ.
\]
Traveling along \(AT\), this boundary arc, and \(UB\) is allowed. Its length is
\[
2(5\sqrt3)+\frac{60}{360}(2\pi\cdot5)
=10\sqrt3+\frac{5\pi}{3}.
\]
We must also show that no allowed path is shorter. Follow any such path from \(A\) to \(B\). Its direction from \(O\) changes between opposite rays, so it must pass, in order, through the two tangent rays on one side of the circle, possibly making additional turns. Call the corresponding path points \(P\) and \(Q\), on rays \(OT\) and \(OU\).

The portion before \(P\) has length at least \(AP\), which is at least \(AT\), because \(AT\) is perpendicular to line \(OT\). Similarly, the portion after \(Q\) has length at least \(UB\).

For the middle portion, move every point radially inward onto the circle. This cannot increase length. Here is the elementary distance comparison behind that fact. For outside points \(X,Y\) with \(OX\ge OY\ge5\), move \(X\) inward to \(Z\) with \(OZ=OY\). The perpendicular foot of \(Y\) on line \(OX\) lies at or before \(Z\), so the Pythagorean theorem gives \(XY\ge ZY\). Scaling \(Z\) and \(Y\) together by \(5/OY\le1\) then puts them on the circle and shortens their distance again. Thus radial projection cannot increase any chord length, and consequently cannot increase path length.

The projected middle portion joins \(T\) to \(U\) along the circle, so it is at least the shorter arc length \(5\pi/3\). Every allowed path therefore has length at least
\[
AT+\frac{5\pi}{3}+UB
=10\sqrt3+\frac{5\pi}{3}.
\]
Our constructed route attains this bound. The shortest length is \(\boxed{10\sqrt3+\frac{5\pi}{3}}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
